title: #20 An idea to improve topic-specific revision
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Craig Barton critiques the common revision-lesson pattern of telling students up front which topic a set of practice questions covers, arguing that doing so removes an authentic exam skill: figuring out what a question is actually asking without being told. He proposes presenting the same struggling-topic questions at the start of the lesson with no topic label, then challenging students to identify the topic themselves and articulate how they knew, before working through the material as normal. He extends the idea with his SSDD Problems framework (Same Surface, Different Deep), sets of problems that share surface features like an image or number set but actually draw on different areas of the curriculum, forcing students to look past superficial cues. Both moves are framed as guards against the "illusion of mastery" that comes from students completing exercises after already being told exactly which topic they belong to.
points: Announcing the topic of a revision worksheet upfront removes students' opportunity to practise the genuinely difficult exam skill of identifying what a question is asking without being told.

Presenting the same struggling-topic questions unlabeled at the start of a lesson, and asking students to identify the topic and justify their reasoning, converts a routine revision task into authentic retrieval practice.
The SSDD Problems framework (Same Surface, Different Deep) uses visually or numerically similar question sets that actually test different curriculum areas, forcing students below surface features.
Barton frames unlabeled practice as a defense against "illusion of mastery," the false confidence that comes from completing questions once told exactly what topic they belong to.
quotes: This is all good. But the problem students often face in exams is identifying exactly what topic a given question relates to.

Announcing this is a Pythagoras lesson, or labelling the booklet of questions or worksheet as such, robs students of an important opportunity to practise such identification, and can lead to an illusion of mastery where we assume that if they can successfully complete the questions in the lesson then the topic is no longer an issue.
Present students with the same set of questions at the start of the lesson, but with no hints or cues, and challenge them to identify the topic.
This can spice up the start of the lesson and help students get better at determining what exam questions are really asking.
SSDD stands for Same Surface (structure), Different Deep (structure).

The idea is that such sets of questions force students to delve below the surface features and to think hard about what the question is really asking, as well as tapping into the benefits of retrieval practice.
